title: Modernisation Fund: Green or Gas?
content:
In July 2026, as Europe — the world’s fastest-warming continent — grappled with record-breaking heatwaves threatening public health, infrastructure and economic productivity, the United States’ war with Iran once again exposed the European Union’s vulnerability to volatile imported fossil fuel prices. The spike added €47 billion to the bloc’s fossil fuel import bill in just three months and reignited debate over the future of the European Union’s Emissions Trading System, now emerging as a crucial test of the credibility of the bloc’s climate agenda.

At the heart of that debate is the Modernisation Fund, a large-scale financial instrument financed through the auctioning of carbon emission allowances. During its first five years of operation, from 2021 to 2025, the Fund disbursed more than €20 billion to modernise energy systems and improve energy efficiency in the European Union’s lower-income member states.

content:

title: How the Eastern Flank Views Ukraine and Moldova’s EU Future
content:
The European Council’s decision to grant candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova in 2022, followed by the opening of accession negotiations, reflected a growing recognition that enlargement had become not merely a policy instrument but also a strategic response to Russian aggression.

This report compares the positions of nine EU member states on the Union’s Eastern Flank – Bulgaria, Czechia, Finland, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, and Slovakia – highlighting both the substantial degree of strategic convergence and the important differences that continue to shape the debate over the European Union’s next enlargement.

title: Did the Ukrainian embassy instruct Ukrainians to record Poles?
content:
Political tensions in Poland and public debate have become increasingly strained in recent weeks. Social media has seen a growing number of videos and headlines fuelling hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. At the centre of the latest controversy is the Ukrainian embassy, which, according to widely shared online claims, allegedly issued official instructions telling its citizens how to secretly record Poles, provoke them and portray them negatively online.

A closer examination of these claims and verification of the original sources, however, paints a very different picture, revealing a classic case of disinformation.

title: NATO’s eastward expansion explained: How Russia’s words helped convince a hesitant America
content:
Pro-Kremlin propaganda has long claimed that NATO broke an alleged promise not to expand eastward. Vladimir Putin himself invoked this narrative to justify Russia’s actions on the eve of the invasion of Ukraine: “There were promises to our country not to expand NATO even one inch to the east. I repeat – they deceived us, in other words, they simply conned us.”

Politicians sympathetic to Moscow – including some in Slovakia – have echoed this version of events. “The Russians are right. The West repeatedly deceived them, for example over NATO enlargement. Russia is now fighting for its security guarantees,” the Slovak prime minister Robert Fico once said in an interview with the controversial Slovak outlet Hlavné správy.

Historians and security experts have repeatedly debunked this claim, pointing out that no written agreement of this kind was ever signed. This was later confirmed by the first and last president of the Soviet Union, Mikhail Gorbachev.

A deeper perspective on these events comes from the prominent American diplomat Ronald D. Asmus, one of the architects of NATO enlargement and a key adviser to former U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

title: Below the Threshold: How Russia Is Testing NATO Without Starting a War
content:
Kevin Riehle spent more than three decades working in US national security and now lectures on intelligence and security at Brunel University of London. His specialist field is Russian intelligence services and covert operations — the institutions and methods operating between routine espionage and open war.

When Russian drones or military aircraft enter or approach NATO airspace, he says, the immediate purpose may be reconnaissance: measuring detection times, identifying which institutions respond and observing how political leaders describe the incident.

“Essentially, Russia is testing the boundaries,” Riehle says. It wants to discover not only what NATO can detect, but what it will tolerate. The question is when the Alliance decides that enough is enough.

Russia has long cast itself as the injured or encircled party rather than the aggressor. A forceful response to a limited airspace violation could therefore be absorbed into the Kremlin’s narrative that NATO started the confrontation.

title: Polish citizens call for reform of hunting legislation
content:
For the first time in many years, opponents of the current hunting system are trying to change the law not through the activities of civil society organisations or further petitions, but by using a tool of direct democracy. The Citizens’ Legislative Initiative Committee “Attention! Hunting. Let’s Change Hunting Law. For Good” has started collecting the 100,000 signatures required to submit a citizens’ bill amending the Hunting Law to the Sejm.

The authors of the bill want to change the way the hunting system operates. They propose mandatory periodic medical and psychological examinations for all hunters possessing firearms, the creation of a public hunting register, an obligation for the Polish Hunting Association to publish its financial reports, and the abolition of so-called commercial hunting.

As Katarzyna Jaślar from the Akcja Demokracja Foundation, which is involved in collecting signatures for the initiative, told FocusEurope.pl, conversations with citizens show that many people are unaware of the current rules governing hunting.

title: In Latvia, with ladders; in Lithuania, through tunnels: MP’s concern proves justified
content:
“It is no surprise that Lithuania is criticising Latvia’s inability to deal with migrants and threatening to restore border checks,” the MP wrote.

Petraviča published the post on 15 July, while Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs was on a state visit to Lithuania. A few days earlier, Lithuania’s new interior minister, Martīns Katelīns, had raised the possibility of temporarily restoring border controls with Latvia because secondary irregular migration was increasing. Compared with the first half of last year, the flow had reportedly quadrupled — from just over 300 to more than 1,200 migrants, the LETA news agency reported.

Rinkēvičs described the possible restoration of border controls as a catastrophe, noting that substantial resources would have to be diverted from the external border to monitor the internal one. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda indirectly agreed, telling journalists that restoring border controls with Latvia would amount to capitulating to irregular migration, according to LETA.

title: “Quality multiplied by quantity”: Poland aims to build a powerful, large-scale army
content:
The Polish government has enshrined the need for significantly stronger military capabilities in an ambitious plan to build the largest and most modern army in Europe within the next 15 years.

The government’s strategic objective of creating an armed force numbering as many as 500 000 personnel has this year been incorporated into the Polish Armed Forces Development Programme for 2025-2039. The document, widely discussed in the Polish media, envisages not only a dramatic increase in troop numbers but also a technological revolution through the large-scale introduction of drones and artificial intelligence systems.

As the newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza points out, the document redefines the country’s approach to national defence by abandoning the long-standing dilemma of “quality versus quantity”. Instead, it introduces the concept of “quality multiplied by quantity”. This means that the planned expansion of the armed forces must go hand in hand with improving soldiers’ training and professional competence.

One of the key pillars of the new paradigm is the use of technology and innovation as the principal instruments of warfare.
